content: The XENDOS study, along with seven other long-term multicenter, double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical trials lasting one to two years, evaluated the effects of orlistat on weight loss and weight maintenance. During the first year of therapy in the two-year studies, the primary focus was on assessing weight loss and weight maintenance. In the second year, some studies continued to evaluate weight loss and maintenance, while others examined the impact of orlistat on weight regain. The majority of patients in these studies had obesity-related risk factors and comorbidities. In the XENDOS study, which included 3,304 patients aged 30 to 58 years (55% women, 99% Caucasian, 1% other), the time to onset of type 2 diabetes was assessed in addition to weight management. In all studies, treatment with orlistat was compared to placebo, with both groups following a reduced-calorie diet. The diet was designed to reduce caloric intake by approximately 20% and provide 30% of calories from fat. All patients also received nutritional counseling. After one year of treatment, the mean percentage weight loss difference between orlistat-treated and placebo-treated patients was 3%. Among those who completed one year of treatment, 57% of orlistat-treated patients (120 mg three times daily) and 31% of placebo-treated patients achieved at least a 5% reduction in baseline body weight. The percentages of patients achieving ≥5% and ≥10% weight loss after one year were reported in five large multicenter studies for the intent-to-treat populations. Relative changes in obesity-associated risk factors after one year of therapy with orlistat and placebo were analyzed for the entire population and for those with abnormal baseline values. In the overall population, pooled data from five clinical studies showed improvements in metabolic, cardiovascular, and anthropometric risk factors associated with obesity, regardless of baseline risk factor status. One year of orlistat therapy resulted in significant relative improvements in several risk factors, including fasting insulin levels and waist circumference, particularly in patients with abnormal baseline values. Three studies specifically evaluated the effects of orlistat compared to placebo in reducing weight regain after prior weight loss. In two studies (14119C and 14185), patients had previously lost weight through one year of orlistat treatment combined with a mildly hypocaloric diet. In another study (14302), patients who had lost at least 8% of their body weight in the previous six months through diet alone were treated with orlistat for one year to assess its effects on weight regain. The diet during the weight regain phase was a weight-maintenance diet, and patients received less nutritional counseling compared to the weight-loss studies. Long-term results from four of the five one-year weight management studies demonstrated that orlistat was more effective than placebo in maintaining weight loss over two years. At the end of the first year, patients' diets were reviewed and adjusted as needed. In the second year, the prescribed diet aimed to maintain the patients' current weight. Orlistat consistently showed superior efficacy compared to placebo in long-term weight control in these large, multicenter, two-year, double-blind, placebo-controlled studies.
